Australian Barley Export Tariffs Prompt Industry Uncertainty and Site Slowdowns

Australia’s agricultural sector is grappling with the impact of China’s newly introduced tariffs on Australian barley exports, with industry sources reporting operational slowdowns and heightened uncertainty across major grain-producing regions.

The 40% import tariff, announced by Chinese authorities earlier this month and effective immediately, has led to a significant drop in export orders for Australian barley. China has traditionally accounted for nearly 70% of Australia’s barley exports, making the abrupt policy shift especially disruptive for growers and exporters in Western Australia, South Australia, and New South Wales.

Local barley processor Riverland Grains reported a 45% decrease in export volumes compared to the same period last year. CEO James Lockhart stated, “We have idle capacity at our Geraldton and Port Augusta sites, with reduced shifts for processing workers. Some casual staff have not been rostered for the past two weeks.”

The National Farmers Union of Australia (NFUA) estimates that more than 2,000 seasonal and permanent jobs are at risk across the barley supply chain. “We’re seeing immediate impacts on rural employment and farm cashflow,” said NFUA President Sally Griffin. “Growers are holding unsold stock, and uncertainty is affecting planting decisions for 2025.”

Grain analyst Peter Wong of MarketAgro projected that farm gate barley prices could fall by as much as 35% over the next quarter if the tariff remains in place. “There’s been a sharp correction in local prices since the announcement,” Wong noted. “Producers are facing tough decisions about storage, forward selling, and crop diversification.”

Industry groups are urging the Australian government to pursue dialogue with Chinese counterparts, warning that prolonged restrictions could have long-term implications for regional investment and farm viability. The Department of Agriculture confirmed ongoing talks but cautioned that “a resolution may take time.”

With the export window for the current harvest narrowing, the outlook for Australia’s barley sector remains uncertain as the tariff dispute enters its third week.
